lessons.title: Research and learning
lessons.html:
Featured task: a research digest with a claim ledger. Start with a narrow question, date range, and allowed source types. Search broadly, but open the original source behind every important claim.

Build a digest that someone can audit

A reader wants to know what changed this week, not merely which headlines an assistant found. Your digest needs selection criteria and a trail back to the sources.

Define the topic and period, gather a small source set, and deduplicate repeated stories. Ask for the central claim of each item and the passage supporting it. Then write a synthesis that distinguishes developments from commentary and speculation.

For academic work, an exploratory scan maps themes and possible sources. A systematic review requires a documented method appropriate to the research question. Do not upgrade the label just because the assistant searched many pages. Product examples in the directory can help find material; you still own inclusion and interpretation.

Follow the example

Deliverable: five items, each with a date, two-sentence summary, original link, relevance note, and one uncertainty. A copied press release counts as one underlying source even if it appears on several sites.

What should you do with an interesting claim whose source cannot be opened?

Exclude it from verified findings or clearly label it unverified. Do not let an attractive headline lower the evidence threshold.

Distinguish an initial literature scan (map themes, identify candidate sources, note gaps) from a systematic review (pre-defined inclusion criteria, documented search, dual screening when required). Do not label a quick scan as a systematic review.

Mini-workflow

  1. Collect three sources with author, publisher, date, and link.
  2. Draft a 120-word digest that distinguishes agreement, disagreement, and unknowns.
  3. Create a ledger: claim, supporting passage, source date, status, and reviewer note.
  4. Remove claims that the cited passage does not actually support.

OUTPUT

A dated digest plus a source ledger. Specify actual inputs (question, sources, dates) and output (digest + ledger)-not a generic “cited brief.”

lessons.title: Writing and communication
lessons.html:
Edit without adding facts. The email and plain-language examples use Notice v2: 15 October, 14:00-16:00, Room 204, up to 20 participants, AMD 10,000, registration open, no deadline specified, and staff approval required for a seat. For the meeting minutes, use only the supplied notes below.

One source, several audiences

A staff email, a public post, and a plain-language notice can sound different while carrying exactly the same facts. The skill is adapting the expression without inventing content.

Create a fact sheet before asking for variants. Mark dates, amounts, conditions, and unknowns. Then specify the audience and purpose for each version. Request a change log when you need to see whether the assistant added a claim.

Meeting minutes need special care. A notice may state a fee, but that does not prove a meeting decided it. Use the actual notes for decisions and action owners; keep missing decisions visible. An assistant should not turn vague discussion into official commitments.

Follow the example

Source notes: 'Discussed an AI event; no date agreed.' A faithful minute says the date remains undecided. It must not borrow a date from a different event just to complete the template.

What stays fixed when the audience changes?

The supported facts, conditions, and uncertainty. Tone, detail, and structure may change; evidence does not.

Email before

Hi, workshop soon, join ASAP or miss out!

Email after

Hello colleagues, registration is open for the 15 October workshop (Room 204, up to 20 places). A seat is confirmed after staff approval.

Original meeting notes

People talked about AI and maybe fees.

Source-faithful minutes

AI and possible fees were discussed. The notes do not record a fee decision, action owner, or deadline. Confirm those details with the participants.

Complex wording

Capacity constraints require provisional enrollment confirmation.

Plain language, checked against the notice

There are up to 20 places. Your place is confirmed only after staff approval.

A fee stated in a notice does not prove that a meeting made a fee decision. Changing the audience changes the tone, not the facts. A named approver checks the exact text before it is sent.

lessons.title: Presentations and visual design
lessons.html:
Featured task: one annotated slide. Build the message from approved facts before asking for layout. Keep Armenian words as editable text outside generated images so spelling, accessibility, and search remain under human control.

Make the message visible before making it beautiful

A slide titled 'Strong progress' can conceal a misleading chart. A slide titled 'Five of twenty places are confirmed' gives the audience a claim they can inspect.

Build a slide around one message, one relevant visual, and the evidence needed to interpret it. Label units, time periods, and denominators. For bar charts, a zero baseline usually supports honest magnitude comparison. Keep pending, cancelled, and confirmed registrations distinct.

Use a slide assistant for layout and variation after the argument is checked. Keep Armenian headings as editable text, not baked into generated images. Provide readable labels, contrast, and an accessible description of the chart's meaning.

Follow the example

Use the registration data to make a five-slide sequence: purpose, confirmed attendance, fee status, unresolved requests, and the decision needed. Do not fill five slides with five different versions of the same headline.

Why should the slide include the denominator 20?

Five confirmations means little without capacity. The denominator lets the reader interpret 5/20 as 25% rather than confusing counts with percentages.

APPLY THE LECTURE KNOWLEDGE

Design a visual brief before generating a visual

A useful visual brief names the audience, purpose, key message, format, hierarchy, required facts, exclusions, and accessibility needs. For an infographic, first decide which claims and numbers are approved; then choose the chart or illustration. A text model can help clarify the brief, but it should not invent the facts the visual is meant to communicate.

Image style language can make a direction more precise: subject, setting, composition, mood, color, camera or illustration treatment, and what to avoid. Do not ask a system to imitate a living artist for publication. Prefer original descriptive language and review the result for rights, labels, and factual integrity.

Try it with a safe example

Write a brief for a fictional course poster: audience, one approved date, one call to action, visual hierarchy, alt text idea, and three things the image must not imply.

Check before you continue

Use a real chart for exact quantities. An image generator is not a reliable data-visualization engine.

Workshop registrations

5 confirmed / 20 capacity

Annotation: denominator is total capacity; source is Notice v2 + registration table.

Հայերեն խմբագրելի տեքստ․ 5 հաստատված մասնակցություն՝ 20 հնարավոր տեղից։

Repair the misleading chart

A cropped axis makes 5 confirmed registrations look almost equal to capacity. Redraw from zero, label both values, and state that two pending requests are not confirmed.

lessons.title: Video audio and music
lessons.html:
Media work is a chain, not a one-click generation. Choose the route that matches the output.

Make a short film or song as a production process

Generating a clip is only one stage of making a film. A useful 30-second video needs a message, continuity, understandable sound, captions, and permission to publish its materials.

Start with a brief: audience, purpose, length, tone, and facts that must not change. Write a script and divide it into shots. Generate or record short pieces, then edit them into a coherent sequence. Check continuity, pronunciation, subtitles, and any synthetic elements that should be disclosed.

For music, use an original concept and lyrics you are permitted to use. A tool such as Suno can help explore arrangements, but the account's current terms and your intended use still matter. Avoid unauthorized voice cloning or misleading imitation. Keep a production log of inputs, licenses, edits, and approval.

Follow the example

A campus video can use three shots: a question from a student, a visual demonstration, and a closing invitation. A song exercise can use an original four-line chorus about curiosity. Review the words before generating many versions; otherwise you pay to polish the wrong message.

What makes a media draft ready to share?

The message is accurate, edits are coherent, accessibility is addressed, rights are checked for the intended use, and an accountable person approves the final version.

APPLY THE LECTURE KNOWLEDGE

Plan multimedia as a production workflow

Video, voice, music, and animation are not simply longer text. Define the intended audience, duration, script or storyboard, permitted source materials, voice or visual rights, review points, and final format. A short test clip can reveal problems with pacing, pronunciation, captions, character consistency, or factual claims before you generate a full version.

When a work represents real people, places, events, or a community, take extra care with consent, accuracy, and context. Label synthetic material where relevant. Never let an attractive soundtrack, fluent narration, or vivid clip substitute for a source check.

Try it with a safe example

Create a 20-second fictional public-service video brief with six storyboard beats, an on-screen source line, captions, and a human review before publication.

Check before you continue

If a name, date, or claim is essential, verify it in the script and on screen after rendering.

Videobrief → factual script → shot list → generated or filmed clips → edit → captions → disclosure
Audioapproved text → consented voice → pronunciation pass → edit → transcript → accessibility check
Musicoriginal concept → lyric check → generations → human selection → rights/plan review → credit

Do not clone a person’s voice or imitate a living artist without authorization. Keep a production log identifying synthetic elements, licensed inputs, and the person who approved publication.

lessons.title: Personal productivity
lessons.html:
Featured task: repair a fictional workday. An assistant schedules nine hours of tasks into 08:30–16:30, overlaps lunch with a call, and leaves no travel or review time. The goal is not a prettier calendar; it is a feasible one.

Repair a plan instead of accepting its confidence

The most useful AI planning exercise may be finding why a proposed day cannot work. Constraints make the answer checkable.

List fixed commitments, task durations, travel, breaks, and review time. Compare the sum with the available hours. Ask the assistant to show conflicts before proposing a revised plan. You decide what to defer; do not allow it to silently remove an obligation.

Use planning for low-risk support, such as study blocks or household tasks. Facts about transport, prices, or opening hours still require a current check. A tidy calendar is not evidence of feasibility.

Follow the example

If nine hours of work must fit into an eight-hour day before lunch and travel, ask for the minimum set of tasks to defer and the consequence of each choice. Reject a plan that merely overlaps them.

Who decides which task loses priority?

The person responsible for the commitments. AI can make the trade-offs visible, not own the consequences.

Pass criteria: no overlap, fixed commitments preserved, one demanding task deferred, two short buffers, and the human owner chooses the trade-off.

lessons.title: Data and analysis
lessons.html:
Featured task: check a small dataset before interpreting it.

From a table to a defensible conclusion

An assistant sees rising revenue and calls a campaign successful. It may not know that the price changed, a duplicate row exists, or the figures cover different periods.

Check the dataset before asking for insight. Identify units, time periods, missing values, duplicates, and category definitions. Reproduce key counts and totals with a spreadsheet or code you can inspect. Separate a description of the data from a causal explanation.

Ask for a small output: one checked table, one appropriate chart, and three conclusions with limitations. Do not accept a confident story that the data cannot distinguish from alternative explanations.

Follow the example

Week 1 has four confirmations and week 2 has five. You can describe the increase of one. Without additional evidence, you cannot attribute it to an advertisement, teacher quality, or a policy change.

Why keep row identifiers?

They let you trace a total back to its records, find duplicates, and explain corrections instead of trusting an opaque summary.

APPLY THE LECTURE KNOWLEDGE

Treat AI data analysis as a transparent analytical process

An assistant may write and run code, but you still need to define the question, inspect the data, choose the denominator and metric, and verify the result. Ask it to describe the columns, missing values, time range, transformations, and assumptions before interpreting a chart. Keep the source file and analysis steps available for review.

Use AI to explore a spreadsheet, create a first graph, or suggest questions. Do not accept a trend as a causal explanation without evidence. Recalculate key numbers independently, inspect unusual values, and label a chart with units, time period, sample, and limitations.

Try it with a safe example

For a fictional sales table, ask for column definitions, a list of missing values, monthly total revenue, one chart, and a sentence separating an observed pattern from a possible explanation.

Check before you continue

A calculation produced by code is still a result to review: verify the file, formula, units, filters, and chart labels.

WeekConfirmed (people)Capacity (people)Paid (AMD)
142020,000
252025,000
352025,000

State the unit and denominator: week 3 occupancy is 5/20 = 25%, not “5%.” Paid AMD is not participant count. Three rows cannot establish a trend or cause.

lessons.title: Business marketing and sales
lessons.html:
Featured task: a business claim sheet. Separate evidence from copy before writing a campaign.

Separate the offer from the evidence

A persuasive draft says your course is the most effective in Armenia. If you cannot support that comparison, stronger copy has created a weaker claim.

Build a claim sheet before a campaign: proposed claim, supporting source, permitted wording, uncertainty, and reviewer. Use AI for alternative messages, audience questions, and content plans. Keep claims about outcomes, rankings, savings, or guarantees tied to appropriate evidence.

For sales, draft from known customer needs rather than inferred sensitive traits. For business planning, separate estimates from measured results. A generated market size or conversion forecast is not research until its assumptions and sources are checked.

Follow the example

Replace 'Guaranteed career transformation' with a supported description: 'Four instructor-led sessions with guided practice and feedback', if that is what the course actually provides.

Can a disclaimer rescue an unsupported headline?

Do not rely on it. Rewrite the main claim to match the evidence and have the final message reviewed.

Proposed claimRequired evidenceStatusAllowed wording
“Most popular workshop”Comparable enrollment dataMissingReject
“Up to 20 places”Notice v2 ASupportedUse with source
“Guaranteed career results”Longitudinal outcome studyMissingReject

Sales or marketing review asks “what proves this exact sentence?” Brand fit never substitutes for substantiation.

lessons.title: Education people and management
lessons.html:
AI can support education and management, but support material is different from a decision about a person.

Support a person without deciding for them

Drafting practice questions and assigning a final grade are not the same kind of task. One supports teaching; the other affects a person's outcome.

Use AI to help prepare lesson examples, feedback drafts, meeting summaries, or rubric wording from approved material. Have the responsible professional check accuracy, level, and fairness. Do not turn generated judgments into automatic grading, recruitment, promotion, or disciplinary decisions.

Give people a way to understand and challenge consequential decisions. Protect personal data and follow the institution's authorized process. A model can summarize evidence, but it cannot assume the authority or responsibility of the teacher, manager, or committee.

Follow the example

Ask for three practice questions from a public lesson and check the answer key yourself. Do not upload identifiable student work to an unapproved service or use its score as the final grade.

What makes an AI feedback draft useful?

It points to specific evidence, matches the rubric, suggests an achievable next step, and is checked by the accountable educator before delivery.

Appropriate support

  • Draft practice questions from an approved lesson.
  • Suggest rubric wording for teacher review.
  • Summarize anonymous team themes.

Human decision required

  • Assign a final grade.
  • Rank job candidates.
  • Decide promotion, discipline, or dismissal.

For people decisions, use authorized evidence, due process, a named accountable decision-maker, and a way to challenge errors. Do not infer sensitive traits.

lessons.title: Coding automation and agents
lessons.html:
Choose one of two routes; both require tests.

A working demo is the beginning of testing

An assistant writes a formula that works on the example row. The real spreadsheet contains blanks, duplicate names, and unexpected values. The first success has not tested those cases.

Describe expected behavior before asking for code. Supply sample inputs and expected outputs, including at least one edge case. Ask for an explanation and test the result in a disposable environment without secrets or production access.

For larger changes, require version control, review, tests, logs, and a rollback plan. An agent that can edit files or call services needs explicit boundaries. Code that runs is not necessarily correct, secure, accessible, or maintainable.

Follow the example

For a fee-total formula, test confirmed, pending, cancelled, and blank status values. Define whether a duplicate identifier should be rejected before computing a total. Compare with a manual calculation.

What should you do if you cannot explain what generated code accesses?

Do not run it with sensitive files or credentials. Ask for an explanation and qualified review, or reduce the task to something you can inspect.

APPLY THE LECTURE KNOWLEDGE

Build the smallest useful app first

A good first AI-built app has one clear goal, a few known inputs, an observable output, and no unnecessary external connections. State the user flow, error cases, privacy boundary, and acceptance checks. A simple calculator, quiz, planner, or static prototype teaches more safely than a complex multi-user system with live data.

Generate in small increments: interface sketch, one working interaction, validation, then refinement. Open and use the result yourself. Test empty, incorrect, and edge-case inputs. Do not assume generated code is secure, accessible, maintainable, or ready to publish simply because it runs once.

Try it with a safe example

Write a build brief for a fictional study-break calculator: goal, two numeric inputs, one result, one validation rule, an empty-state message, and a statement that no data is stored.

Check before you continue

Before sharing an AI-built page, test its stated acceptance checks and have a person review any action, data collection, or public claim.

Beginner route

Ask for a formula or small webpage. Use sample data, request comments, test three normal cases and two edge cases, then explain the result in your own words.

Technical route

Define repository context, interfaces, permissions, test suite, logs, rollback, and code review. Give an agent the minimum tools and require approval before external changes.

Never run unfamiliar code with secrets or production access merely because it looks plausible. A working demo is not production readiness.

lessons.title: Creative culture and public value
lessons.html:
Featured task: Armenian cultural or public value. Start with community context, approved terminology, accessible Armenian, and the rights of people represented-not with a generic visual style.

Local context is part of accuracy

A grammatically correct Armenian public notice can still use the wrong place name, an inappropriate tone, or a confusing institutional title. Translation alone does not provide cultural understanding.

Work from community-approved facts and terminology. Identify the people represented, the audience, the practical action, and the reviewer. For cultural materials, record sources and avoid treating generated imagery as historical evidence. For public notices, prioritize clarity, accessibility, and uncertainty over novelty.

Use fictional scenarios for practice and label them prominently. Do not turn a training emergency into a message that could be mistaken for a real warning. Real public-safety content requires current verified contacts and approval from the responsible authority.

Follow the example

For a museum description, ask the assistant to simplify an approved text and preserve Armenian names. Keep disputed dates labeled as disputed. Use generated illustrations only when clearly identified as interpretations, not archival records.

What should happen to a guessed emergency contact?

Remove it. In a real notice, obtain the verified contact from the responsible authority; in a fictional exercise, state that no real contact should be used.

Fictional emergency exercise

Training scenario only: water service in the fictional village of Arevik is interrupted from 10:00 to 16:00. The municipality has not announced a cause. No real emergency contact is supplied in this fictional exercise.

Draft a calm Armenian notice, an English accessibility version, and 160-character SMS. Preserve uncertainty about the cause, label the village fictional, and require municipal approval. Generated imagery must not depict real victims or recognizable residents.

PUBLIC-VALUE CHECK

Correct language, source fidelity, accessibility, cultural context, and accountable approval matter more than novelty.

lessons.title: Four projects step by step
lessons.html:
These are optional walkthroughs, not additional required projects. Each shows the same correction loop.

Follow the correction, not just the finished artifact

A finished presentation hides the most educational part: the mistake someone noticed and repaired. These walkthroughs make that work visible.

For each project, preserve five stages: input, prompt, first output, correction, and accepted artifact. State the acceptance test before generating. Compare the corrected version with both the source and the first attempt.

You do not need to complete all four projects. Choose the one whose checking method you can understand, then transfer that method to a different task. The point is not producing more files; it is learning how an output becomes trustworthy enough for its intended use.

Follow the example

In the registration-slide project, the first draft counts pending applicants as confirmed. The correction restores the status filter and denominator. The final slide is accepted only after its values reproduce the table.

Which project artifact is most useful for explaining your learning?

The before/after pair with a source-based explanation of the correction. A polished final file alone cannot show how it was checked.

WORKED STUDIO · TRY, COMPARE, TRANSFER

Finish one small artifact: a three-slide decision brief

A catalogue is a menu, not a requirement to try every item. Choose a task with available input, a visible output, and a check you can perform. Here we turn fictional survey data into a short presentation. You can complete the reasoning on paper; using a presentation or image tool is optional. This studio sits inside the existing applications chapter, not a new mandatory project.

Your source packet

Fictional neighbourhood reading-club survey
20 people responded once each. Preferred format: discussion 10; practical workshop 6; film evening 4.
Budget for a pilot: AMD 25,000. Venue capacity: 12.
No respondent age, availability, or willingness to attend was collected.
Goal: recommend one format for a small pilot and explain what still needs confirmation. Do not claim these 20 responses represent the whole neighbourhood.

A prompt you can adapt

Create a three-slide decision brief using only the survey. Slide 1: the preference counts with an honest title and denominator. Slide 2: one pilot recommendation and its limits. Slide 3: the next checks and a human decision owner, marked 'to assign' because none is supplied. Provide chart labels and a text description. Do not invent quotes, demographic findings, prices, or attendance commitments.

  1. Verify the numbers before designing

    10 + 6 + 4 = 20 responses. The shares are 50%, 30%, and 20%. Discussion is the largest category, but 50% is not more than half. Use a bar chart beginning at zero with the same scale for all categories. Do not draw 10 as five times larger than 6 through a distorted axis.

  2. Write the argument before choosing a theme

    Slide 1 answers 'What did these respondents prefer?' Slide 2 answers 'What small test could we try?' Slide 3 answers 'What must we confirm before committing?' This sequence connects evidence to a proposal without pretending the survey already proves demand, cost, or attendance. A dramatic template cannot fix a missing argument.

  3. Choose tools for a bounded role

    An approved assistant can draft titles and speaker notes. A spreadsheet can calculate counts and shares. A presentation editor can arrange the slides; the maintained directory lists examples. Use real chart values rather than asking an image generator to draw exact labels. If you add an illustration, label it illustrative and keep it separate from the data chart.

  4. Review the artifact as the audience will use it

    Check that the title says 'among 20 respondents', labels remain readable on a small screen, and the chart has a text description. The recommendation must respect the 12-person capacity. A preference for discussion is not a confirmed reservation. Verify venue, actual costs, date, accessible participation, and recruitment before a human approves the pilot.

A worked result, not a live AI response

Slide 1: 'Discussion leads among 20 respondents' - 10 discussion, 6 workshop, 4 film; fictional convenience sample. Slide 2: 'Test one discussion session for up to 12 people' - a proposal, subject to attendance and budget checks. Slide 3: 'Confirm before booking' - venue, date, itemized costs within AMD 25,000, access needs, and an assigned decision owner. These are reviewable slide contents, not an automatically published deck.

What changes the decision?
ObservationInterpretation
Supported findingDiscussion received 10 of the 20 supplied responses.
Reasonable proposalTest a small discussion session, with feasibility and attendance still to be checked.
Unsupported claimThe whole neighbourhood wants this, or 10 people have confirmed attendance.

Now change one condition

The venue capacity changes from 12 to 8. Which slide should change, and which numbers must remain untouched?

Compare after your own attempt

Change the pilot proposal to up to 8 people and review recruitment or a waiting list. Keep the survey at 20 respondents with counts 10, 6, and 4. Capacity is not the survey denominator. Update the planning checks, not the evidence, to make the proposal fit the new constraint.

Research digest
  1. Input: three dated articles
  2. Prompt: source-only digest prompt
  3. Intermediate: draft repeats one press release twice
  4. Correction: deduplicate and add an independent source
  5. Finished: 120-word digest + ledger
Announcement
  1. Input: Notice v2
  2. Prompt: plain-language prompt
  3. Intermediate: draft invents a deadline
  4. Correction: classify claims and remove unsupported text
  5. Finished: approved bilingual announcement
Registration slide
  1. Input: 8-row table
  2. Prompt: five-slide outline prompt
  3. Intermediate: pending counted as confirmed
  4. Correction: restore status filter and denominator
  5. Finished: annotated five-slide deck
Public SMS
  1. Input: fictional emergency facts
  2. Prompt: short Armenian message prompt
  3. Intermediate: model invents the cause
  4. Correction: state cause unknown and add reviewer
  5. Finished: approved SMS + disclosure

lessons.title: Use the maintained product directory
lessons.html:
There is no second tool-link table here. Tool availability, pricing, privacy terms, and Armenian support change too quickly to maintain duplicate lists.

Keep one maintained source for tool details

Duplicated tool lists drift apart. One may promise a feature that another correctly marks as account-dependent.

Use the Chapter 5 directory as the shared reference, then verify current details on the official website. Record your own task-specific test separately. This keeps the course's teaching stable while product details evolve.

Follow the example

A video project can link to the media category rather than copying a price table into its instructions. The learner then checks the intended plan and publication rights at the time of use.

What should a project keep locally even when it links to the directory?

Its actual tool choice, account context, date, acceptance test, and result. The directory cannot replace the project record.

Use the maintained curated product directory in Chapter 5, Lesson 8. Start with approved tools, check the review date and official source, then test your exact task with permitted data.

lessons.title: Use the searchable companion catalogue
lessons.html:
Search all 100 ideas by task or tool and filter by category. Open a card to inspect its required inputs and expected output. Then use this lesson’s final section to plan your choice.

Search with a task, then inspect the input

Searching 'presentation' gives you possibilities. Reading the required input tells you whether one of them is feasible today.

Filter by category, open an entry, and compare its expected output with your goal. Time and difficulty are planning estimates. They do not include every learner's setup, review, or revision effort. Choose an entry you can verify with your available evidence and skills.

Follow the example

If a news-filtering task requires current articles you do not have, first collect a permitted source set. Do not ask the assistant to invent example news and then treat it as a real digest.

Why inspect the input before choosing the tool?

The input determines evidence needs, sensitivity, and supported formats. A tool cannot compensate for absent permission or nonexistent source material.

lessons.title: Catalogue exercise
lessons.html:
Choose one feasible task. Define the input you are permitted to use, the exact output, one observable acceptance test, and the named reviewer.

Write a brief you can actually evaluate

'Use AI for research' is an intention. 'Produce a five-item digest from three dated sources, with each claim checked' is a task.

Specify permitted input, exact output, observable acceptance test, and reviewer. Add a stop condition if an essential resource is missing. A completed form shows that you entered a plan; it does not automatically prove that the plan is feasible or authorized.

After trying the task, compare expected and actual effort. Keep one error and its correction. That record gives you a better basis for the next attempt than a generic impression that AI was helpful.

Follow the example

Input: public museum hours. Output: a one-day itinerary. Test: every stop is open during the visit, travel time fits, and sources are dated. Reviewer: the traveler. Stop: conflicting hours remain unresolved.

Is rejecting an attractive but unverifiable task a failure?

No. Choosing a lower-risk, checkable task is evidence of good judgment, which is one of the course's main outcomes.

“I lack the data, permission, time, or qualified reviewer” is a valid rejection-not a failure. Choose a lower-risk task instead.

lessons.title: The road ahead
lessons.html:
Your road ahead is personal: notice one recurring task where AI may help, protect the parts that require care and accountable judgment, and improve through small documented trials. Products will change; the habits of framing, checking, correcting, and owning decisions remain useful.

Keep the habits when the products change

The next assistant you use may look different. The questions you ask of it should remain familiar: what is the task, what is the evidence, and who owns the result?

Return to your starting task and compare how you would approach it now. Notice any new boundary you would set or fact you would verify. Progress includes knowing when an ordinary tool or a qualified person is the better choice.

Follow the example

Instead of asking for a finished report immediately, you may now begin with a source list, an outline, and a claim ledger. The final document becomes easier to check.

Which habit will you keep even when you are in a hurry?

Choose a concrete one: verify names and numbers, preserve uncertainty, or require approval before sending. Make it part of your normal workflow.

lessons.title: Your next three steps
lessons.html:
A small experiment for the coming week

You will learn more from one documented trial than from saving another hundred prompts.

Choose a low-risk recurring task, establish the manual baseline, and try one AI-assisted version. Record preparation, generation, review, and correction time separately. Keep the same quality bar. If the result is worse, document why rather than forcing a success story.

Follow the example

Try turning public meeting notes into an action table. Compare missing owners, invented deadlines, and total editing time with your normal method.

When should you expand the experiment?

After the small task passes its checks repeatedly and the owner has approved any new data, users, or actions involved.

  1. This week: choose one low-risk task and write its input, output, acceptance test, and reviewer.
  2. This month: run one controlled comparison, save a failure and correction, and estimate full workflow cost.
  3. This term: teach one colleague TRACE and review your approved tools, data rules, and escalation route.

lessons.title: Overview
lessons.html:
Search English terms and definitions. Confused-term notes distinguish related ideas rather than treating them as synonyms.

Use a term to explain a difference

Knowing a word is useful when it helps you avoid a mistake. 'Training' and 'context' matter because uploading a document is not the same as updating model weights.

Use the glossary while reading rather than memorizing it in isolation. For each unfamiliar term, attach a concrete example and a contrasting idea. Armenian entries retain English equivalents so you can recognize the same concept in product documentation.

Follow the example

Retrieval finds relevant passages. Generation produces a response. A system may do both, but a retrieved passage can still be misinterpreted during generation.

Can you explain one glossary term without using another unexplained term?

Try a familiar example first, then add the technical name. If the explanation remains circular, revisit the lesson where the concept is demonstrated.

AI agent

A system that can plan and take multiple tool-enabled steps within defined permissions.

Algorithm

A defined procedure for performing a task.

Artificial intelligence (AI)

The broad field of systems performing tasks associated with perception, language, prediction, or decision support.

Automation

Software performing a repeatable process with reduced manual effort.

Bias

A systematic distortion. Model bias is measured behavior in a model; societal bias is a wider pattern in institutions or culture. They can interact, but are not synonyms.

Context

Instructions, messages, files, retrieved passages, and tool results available for a response.

Embedding

A numerical representation used to compare meaning or similarity.

Fine-tuning

Additional training that adapts model behavior for particular tasks.

Generative AI

AI that creates text, images, audio, video, code, or other content.

Grounding

Connecting an answer to specified evidence or tool results.

Hallucination

Plausible-looking but unsupported, inaccurate, or fabricated output.

Inference

Using a trained model to produce a prediction or response.

Large language model (LLM)

A model trained on large data collections to process and generate language.

Prompt

Information supplied to guide an AI response or action.

Prompt injection

Untrusted content attempting to redirect an AI system.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Retrieving relevant information into context before generation.

Token

A unit processed by a model, often a word fragment or punctuation.

Training data

Data used to adjust model parameters during training.

Workflow

Ordered inputs, tasks, checks, decisions, and outputs.

lessons.title: Overview
lessons.html:
Choose resources by need. Product interfaces change, so prefer dated official material and test what you read.

Choose a resource for a question

A long reading list is not a learning plan. Start with the question you cannot yet answer and choose the source designed to address it.

Use conceptual teaching material for mechanisms, official product documentation for current features, and institutional guidance for local rules. A framework helps organize thinking; a product help page explains an implementation. Neither automatically answers every question about your situation.

Follow the example

If you are confused about tokens, read a conceptual explanation. If you need the current file limit, open the product's help page for your actual account type.

What should you record when a resource changes your workflow?

The source, date, applicable product or policy, and the specific change you made. Recheck it when those conditions change.

Courses for continued learning

These external courses’ public outlines informed the teaching-design review. EUA examples are original; no affiliation or equivalent certification is implied. Check each site for access conditions.

lessons.title: Suggested learning routine
lessons.html:
Optional routine: weekly, verify one important AI-assisted claim; monthly, retest one saved prompt and read one official update; each term, review approved tools, data rules, accessibility, and approval owners. Keep one failure example and its correction.

Practice retrieval, not just rereading

After a week, try to explain a concept before reopening the lesson. The gap between your explanation and the example tells you what to revisit.

Use short spaced practice: one claim check, one prompt revision, or one calculation. Mix old and new skills instead of practicing only the most recent chapter. Keep a failure notebook with the source, mistaken output, correction, and lesson learned.

Follow the example

This week, revise an email. Next week, check a chart and explain which prompting and verification habits you reused.

What is a useful sign that a habit has transferred?

You recognize the same risk in a different task and apply the check without being told which chapter it came from.

lessons.title: Overview
lessons.html:
Use references as part of the lessons, not as a detached bibliography.

Read a reference for what it actually supports

An influential paper can explain an architecture without proving that your chosen chatbot is safe for confidential student data.

Distinguish research findings, technical documentation, guidance, and legal texts. Each answers different questions and has a different scope. Check dates and read beyond the title. A citation should support the nearby claim, not merely make the page look academic.

Follow the example

Use a transformer paper for architectural background, a product help page for current settings, and your institution's policy for permitted use. Do not substitute one for another.

What makes a reference useful to your reader?

A clear connection to the claim, an accessible original source, and an explanation of its scope and limitations.

Papers - Chapters 1–3

  • Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need: transformer background.
  • Ji et al. (2023), hallucination survey: supports checking claims.
  • Gao et al. (2023), RAG survey: retrieval and grounding.

Technical documentation - Chapters 4–7

  • OpenAI prompt engineering: prompts and evaluation.
  • Anthropic prompt documentation: structured experiments.

Guidance - Chapters 3, 5, 8

  • NIST AI RMF 1.0: risk controls.
  • UNESCO guidance: education and research.

Legislation and policy context - Chapters 5–8

  • EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689. Check applicable Armenian law and institutional policy for your actual work.

lessons.title: Academic integrity and authorship
lessons.html:
Follow institutional rules and disclose material assistance. Cite the underlying evidence, not an AI chat as the source of a fact. The human author remains responsible for claims, citations, originality, permissions, and final judgment.

Disclosure should describe the actual assistance

'AI was used' says very little. A useful disclosure explains which part was assisted and what the human author checked.

Follow the institution's rules and describe material assistance accurately. Distinguish language editing, structural suggestions, code generation, and factual research. Cite the underlying evidence for factual claims; do not cite a chat response as proof that an external fact is true.

Keep authorship responsibility clear. The person sharing the work must be able to explain the claims, sources, corrections, and permissions. Disclosure is not a substitute for checking.

Follow the example

A precise statement is: 'AI suggested an outline and language edits. The author rewrote the argument, verified the cited sources, and approved the final text.' Use it only if it describes what actually happened.

Does disclosure transfer responsibility to the tool?

No. It makes the process more transparent while the human author remains responsible for the work.

Two disclosure examples

Short: “AI assisted with language editing. The author verified all claims and citations and approved the final text.”

Detailed: “On 10 September 2026, [tool/model] produced an initial structure from the author’s notes. The author rewrote the analysis, opened and verified every cited source, removed two unsupported claims, and accepts responsibility for the final work.”

quizzes: A chat answer uses a pasted notice correctly for the date, but invents a speaker name. Which mechanism supplied the date, and what should you do about the speaker?
The date came from the supplied context (or retrieval into context). The speaker name is unsupported: remove it or verify it with another source before use.
What additional information would make an AI workshop summary checkable if it mentions a fee?
An approved source that states the fee (or explicitly says there is no fee), plus a human comparison of the draft against that source.
Which should stay fixed in an A/B prompt test?
Source material, question, model/settings where possible, and scoring criteria. Otherwise the reason for a change is unclear.
A concise prompt omits the required source. Is it better?
Not if omission lowers accuracy. Minimize unnecessary text while preserving required evidence.
Two fluent answers name the same workshop date, but only one invents a registration deadline. What evidence distinguishes them?
Open the governing notice. If no deadline is stated, the invented deadline is unsupported even if the wording is polished.
A draft says “at least 20 participants” while the notice says “up to 20.” How do you classify the claim?
Contradicted. “Up to 20” sets a maximum; “at least 20” sets a minimum. Correct the wording or remove the claim.
An edit makes a paragraph smoother and adds “registration closes 10 October,” which is not in the notice. What should you do?
Reject the attractive addition. Keep clarity improvements that preserve meaning; delete unsupported claims.
A chart bars sum to 100, but an AI extract says “120 participants total.” What is the error type?
Extraction invented a total that does not match the labeled bars. Verify totals against the visual, not the fluent summary.
A tool scores highest on formatting but fails your required privacy gate. Should it win?
No. Pass/fail requirements come first. Attractive formatting cannot override a failed privacy or factual-accuracy condition.
Why is an API optional for beginners choosing a tool?
Most early work can use an approved chat application. An API adds setup and responsibility and is needed only when embedding the model in another workflow.
A form note says to ignore approval and email everyone. What should the workflow do?
Treat the note as untrusted data. Keep approval mandatory, flag the instruction attempt, and do not expand recipients.
After a draft timeout, what prevents a duplicate draft on retry?
Check the persistent record_id and state before creating another draft. Retry the same record; do not invent a second one.
At $2 per million input tokens, what do 2,000 input tokens cost?
The API bill falls but review doubles. Is the workflow cheaper?
Not necessarily. Compare total cost per accepted result, using observed quality and review time.
